introduction: Xenophon, Symposium 2.24–27. Read this controlled course adaptation with the glosses, then revisit its source and historical setting on page three.

The comparison of wine to water nourishing plants follows Socrates in the Symposium. The serving instructions and -μι practice sentences are reconstructed teaching dialogue, not a transcript. The lesson title is a traditional maxim, not a quotation assigned here to Xenophon.
Notice δίδωμι and τίθημι: what is given, what is placed, and who receives it?

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Καλλίας τοὺς φίλους ἐπὶ δεῖπνον καλεῖ. μετὰ δὲ τὸ δεῖπνον οἱ φίλοι πίνουσι καὶ διαλέγονται. ὁ Σωκράτης πάρεστιν· οὐ σιωπᾷ, ἀλλὰ περὶ τοῦ οἴνου λέγει.
Ὁ οἶνος ἡδονὴν δίδωσιν, ἀλλὰ τὸ πολὺ βλάπτει. ὁ Σωκράτης τὰ φυτὰ παράδειγμα τίθησιν. ὀλίγον ὕδωρ τὰ φυτὰ αὔξει· τὸ δὲ πολὺ ὕδωρ κακὸν παρέχει.
Καὶ οἱ ἄνθρωποι μέτρου δέονται. ὁ Σωκράτης οὐ κελεύει πάντας πολὺ πίνειν. μικρὰ ποτήρια καὶ πολλάκις· οὕτως οἱ φίλοι ἡδέως τὴν ἑσπέραν διάγουσιν.
Ἐν τῷ ἡμετέρῳ παραδείγματι ὁ φίλος λέγει· «δὸς τὸ ποτήριον, θὲς δὲ τὸν κρατῆρα ἐν μέσῳ.» ὁ ἕτερος τὸ ποτήριον δίδωσι καὶ τὸν κρατῆρα τίθησιν.
Ἔδοσαν μὲν τὸν οἶνον, ἔθεσαν δὲ τὰ ποτήρια. νῦν οἱ συμπόται λόγους ἀντὶ κραυγῆς ἀκούουσιν. ἡ τῶν φίλων συνουσία οὐ τῷ πλήθει τοῦ οἴνου μόνον κρίνεται.
Τί δίδομεν τοῖς φίλοις; τί τίθεμεν ἐν μέσῳ; οὐ ποτὸν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ λόγον καὶ προσοχήν. ὁ δὲ τοῦ σώματος κύριος καὶ τοῦ ἄλλου ἀκούει.

reading.translation:
Callias invites friends to dinner. After dinner the friends drink and converse. Socrates is present; he does not remain silent but speaks about wine.

Wine gives pleasure, but excess harms. Socrates sets out plants as an example. A little water makes plants grow; too much water causes harm.

People too need measure. Socrates does not urge everyone to drink a great deal. Small cups, and frequently: in this way the friends spend the evening pleasantly.

In our teaching example the friend says, “Give the cup, and put the mixing bowl in the middle.” The other gives the cup and places the mixing bowl.

They gave the wine and placed the cups. Now the fellow drinkers hear conversation instead of shouting. The gathering of friends is not judged by the quantity of wine alone.

What do we give our friends? What do we place in the middle? Not only drink, but also conversation and attention. The person in command of his body also listens to the other person.

sections.title: 1. δίδωμι in the present and imperfect
body: δίδωμι is athematic: its endings attach to the stem without the ordinary thematic ο/ε. The present singular has a long vowel, δίδωμι, δίδως, δίδωσι; the plural has short ο, δίδομεν, δίδοτε, διδόασι.
The imperfect is irregular in the singular: ἐδίδουν, ἐδίδους, ἐδίδου; plural ἐδίδομεν, ἐδίδοτε, ἐδίδοσαν. A gift commonly has a recipient in the dative and an object in the accusative.

sections.title: 2. τίθημι in the present and imperfect
body: τίθημι means “put, place” and follows a long/short vowel pattern: τίθημι, τίθης, τίθησι; τίθεμεν, τίθετε, τιθέασι. It can also mean “set out” an example or proposal.
The imperfect singular is ἐτίθην, ἐτίθεις, ἐτίθει; plural ἐτίθεμεν, ἐτίθετε, ἐτίθεσαν. Contrast τίθησι, someone puts something, with κεῖται, something lies in a location.

sections.title: 3. Aorists: ἔδωκα and ἔθηκα
body: δίδωμι and τίθημι have aorist active singulars in -κα: ἔδωκα, ἔδωκας, ἔδωκε; ἔθηκα, ἔθηκας, ἔθηκε. Their ordinary Attic plurals use shorter stems: ἔδομεν, ἔδοτε, ἔδοσαν; ἔθεμεν, ἔθετε, ἔθεσαν.
These are aorists, not perfects simply because κ appears. The infinitives are δοῦναι and θεῖναι. Aorist participles δούς and θείς identify someone who has given or placed.

sections.title: 4. Commands, infinitives, and future forms
body: Learn a few high-frequency non-indicative forms as a usable set. Present διδόναι and τιθέναι view giving and placing as processes; aorist δοῦναι and θεῖναι view the actions as wholes. Aorist singular commands are δός and θές.

Future forms return to familiar -σω endings: δώσω and θήσω. In the reconstructed serving dialogue, commands direct a particular action. They do not prove that the ancient conversation used these exact words.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Symposium
body: Xenophon’s Symposium stages a dinner and drinking party at Callias’s house, with Socrates among the guests. Conversation, entertainment, humor, and claims about what people value make it a different kind of Socratic portrait from the Memorabilia. A literary banquet is not a stenographic record.

Callias hosts the gathering in honor of the young athlete Autolycus. Across nine chapters, a meal and drinking party become a lively experiment in conversation: music, performance, teasing, and competing claims about what each guest values share the room with serious moral questions. Socrates participates in the playfulness instead of standing outside the party to deliver a lecture.

The guests’ boasts bring beauty, wealth, poverty, and personal accomplishment into discussion. Later, Socrates develops an argument about love that values character and the good of the beloved. Entertainment and reflection continually interrupt and reshape one another. This is Xenophon’s Symposium, a distinct work from Plato’s more familiar dialogue of the same title, with its own characters, structure, and dramatic effects.

Reading invitation: follow the modest drinking proposal in chapter 2 into the exchanges about pride in chapters 3–4, then compare the discussion of love in chapter 8. Does moderation help the gathering become more enjoyable and attentive? Treat the dialogue as a literary presentation of elite sociability, not an audio recording of a dinner. Notice who gets a speaking part and whose service makes the gathering possible.

In 2.24–27 Socrates compares the effects of wine with watering plants and favors small, repeated servings. Our title “Nothing in Excess” is a traditional Greek maxim used as a thematic heading; it is not presented as a quotation from this passage.

sections.title: Read an object: the krater
body: A krater is a vessel for mixing wine and water. Its place in a symposium connects a physical object with the management of a shared occasion: how something is served affects how the gathering proceeds. Museum objects and images provide evidence distinct from literary dialogue.

The linked Metropolitan Museum krater is an Archaic Attic object, earlier than the dramatic setting of Xenophon’s party. It illustrates the vessel type and symposium imagery; it is not Callias’s own mixing bowl.

sections.title: Who gets to converse?
body: A convivial scene includes more people than the speakers whose words are recorded. Serving and entertainment involve labor and unequal status. Ask whose enjoyment structures the evening and whose work makes that enjoyment possible.

The reading’s plant analogy is an ancient argument about moderation, not modern health guidance. Students can analyze the analogy without reenacting the drinking. Does the comparison establish the conclusion, or does it leave questions about different people and circumstances?

sections.title: Host a conversation, not a drinking contest
body: Plan a discussion around a shared object such as a book or an image. Decide how turns will be offered, how someone can decline, and how a quiet participant can enter. Use the lesson’s idea of measure to support attention.

Practice the verbs of giving and placing with harmless classroom objects: give a card, place a book. Explain the difference between δίδωσι and ἔδωκε. The commands in the reading are teaching dialogue, not recorded orders at Callias’s party.
